Chapter 9
Enhanced Switched Technologies

This document replaces Chapter 9 of Todd Lammle, CCNA Certification Study Guide, Volume 2, Exam 200-301 (Sybex, 2020), book pages 251 to 288. It covers Spanning Tree Protocol (STP), the STP versions, Rapid PVST+, bridge ID changes, STP failures, PortFast, BPDU Guard and EtherChannel (LACP and PAgP, Layer 2 and Layer 3). Every difference from the book is tagged and listed in the Changes and Gaps Log.

WHAT THE BOOK SAYS
Learning objectives (from the book). After this chapter you should be able to:
Configure and verify Layer 2 and Layer 3 EtherChannel using LACP (objective 2.4).

Describe why Rapid PVST+ is needed and how it basically works (objective 2.5): root port, root bridge (primary and secondary), other port names, port states (forwarding and blocking), and the benefits of PortFast.
VERIFY

Verification note. The STP examples in this chapter (Figures 9.10 and 9.12 and two new paper labs) were recomputed with a Python script that elects the root bridge, finds root ports by lowest path cost, and picks designated ports by path cost, then bridge ID, then port. The script agrees with the book on the final port roles but found a wrong reasoning step in the book (see Section 9.2.2 and the Gaps Log). Nothing in this document was run on real Cisco hardware or in Packet Tracer. Commands and outputs are copied from the book or written from documentation, so they are marked CHECK where they matter.

Book pages 252 to 259. BOOK

Routers stop loops at Layer 3 with the TTL field. Switches have no such field. If you connect switches in a ring, a broadcast frame can travel round and round forever. STP exists to stop loops at Layer 2 by turning off redundant links, while keeping them ready as backups.

Without STP, redundant switch links cause three problems: broadcast storms, multiple copies of frames, and MAC table thrashing (the same source MAC is seen on different ports again and again). STP uses the spanning-tree algorithm (STA) to build a loop-free tree and blocks the links that are not in the tree.
WHY THIS MATTERS

Redundant links are good design (if one fails, another takes over). STP lets you have the redundancy without the loop. Everything in this chapter is about choosing which links to keep and how fast the switch recovers.
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS

Figure 9.1 shows three switches (S1, S2, S3) joined in a triangle, which is a loop. Figure 9.2 shows the same network with STP: one of the three links is blocked, so the loop is gone. IEEE 802.1D is the default STP on Cisco IOS switches (really the Cisco PVST+ version of it).
9.1.1 Spanning-Tree Terms
| Term | Meaning |

| Root bridge | The switch with the lowest (best) bridge ID. All decisions are made from its point of view. Every port on the root bridge is a designated (forwarding) port. The root bridge never has a root port. |
| Non-root bridge | Every other switch. Each one must have exactly one root port. |
| BPDU | Bridge Protocol Data Unit. The STP message that switches send to each other. It carries the bridge ID. By default a BPDU is sent every 2 seconds (the hello time) out each active port. |
| Bridge ID | 8 bytes: bridge priority plus the switch base MAC address. Default priority is 32768. Lowest wins. |
| Port cost | The cost of one link, based on its speed. Faster link, lower cost. |
| Path cost (root path cost) | The sum of the port costs along the way to the root bridge. |
Bridge port roles
| Role | What it is | Forwards frames? |
| Root port | The one port on a non-root switch with the lowest path cost to the root. Tie: lower upstream bridge ID, then lower upstream port number. | Yes |
| Designated port | The port that has the best (lowest) path to the root on a segment. One per segment. | Yes |
| Non-designated port | Everything left over. In 802.1D this is a blocked port. | No |
| Blocked port (802.1D) | Does not forward. Still listens to BPDUs, drops everything else, never sends frames. | No |
| Alternate port (802.1w) | Connected to a segment where another switch holds the designated port. It is a backup path to the root. | No (discarding) |
| Backup port (802.1w) | Connected to a segment where another port on the same switch is the designated port. | No (discarding) |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Book wording to fix. The book says both alternate and backup ports "correspond to the blocking state of 802.1d". That is right in spirit, but in 802.1w they are roles and the port state is discarding. Cisco's own RSTP document says the old blocking role is split into the alternate and backup roles. UPDATED Verified against Cisco document 24062 (official).
MEMORY TIP

Alternate = another switch is the designated one (alternative path to the root). Backup = same switch, redundant link to the same segment (a backup of my own designated port). Backup ports are rare: they need a hub or shared segment.
Spanning-tree port states (802.1D)
| State | Learns MACs? | Forwards data? | What happens |
| Disabled | No | No | Administratively down. Not part of STP. |
| Blocking | No | No | Only listens to BPDUs. All ports start here at power-up. Prevents loops. |
| Listening | No | No | Listens to BPDUs and prepares to forward. Lasts the forward delay (15 s). |
| Learning | Yes | No | Fills the MAC table but still does not forward data. Lasts 15 s. |
| Forwarding | Yes | Yes | Normal operation. A root port or designated port ends here. |
EXAM CRITICAL

Switches fill the MAC address table only in the learning and forwarding states. Most ports sit in blocking or forwarding. Listening and learning are brief transition states you see after a topology change.
This is why a new host sees an amber light for a long time and may fail to get a DHCP address: the port walks through listening and learning first. The book says this takes almost a minute.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Where 50 seconds comes from. Max age 20 s + listening 15 s + learning 15 s = 50 s (a script confirmed the sum). That is the worst case when a link failure is detected by a missing BPDU. When a port on a directly failed link is lost, only listening plus learning (30 s) applies. Default timers: hello 2 s, forward delay 15 s, max age 20 s (they appear in the book's show output). Cisco documentation was not opened for the 30 s case. CHECK
Convergence

Convergence means every switch port has settled into forwarding or blocking. While 802.1D converges, no data is forwarded. The book advises against editing the STP timers and says the better answer is to stop using 802.1D and move to RSTP. BOOK
Link costs
Port cost is for one link. Path cost is the sum of the port costs to the root. Memorise Table 9.1. BOOK
| Link speed | Cost (short method, book Table 9.1) | Cost (long method) UPDATED |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book teaches only the old 16-bit costs. The newer IEEE 802.1D-2004 costs are 32-bit and scale to fast links (2,000,000, 200,000, 20,000, 2,000). On Cisco switches the default is still the short method, and you change it with spanning-tree pathcost method long. All switches in a domain should use the same method. The exam uses the short numbers (100, 19, 4, 2). Sources: Cisco documentation snippet and Network World article for the Cisco default (secondary); long values from vendor documentation of IEEE 802.1D-2004 (secondary). CHECK
Change and check the cost method CHECK
Switch(config)# spanning-tree pathcost method long
Switch# show spanning-tree summary
- spanning-tree pathcost method long changes the method for the whole switch.
- show spanning-tree summary shows which method is in use (look for the pathcost line).
9.1.2 Spanning-Tree Operations
Book pages 257 to 259. BOOK Use the same simple three-switch network, Figure 9.3. All links are 1 Gb/s (cost 4). All priorities are 32768.
| Switch | Bridge priority | MAC address |
The three-step method (book page 265, used for every problem)
- Find the root bridge: lowest bridge ID (priority first, then MAC).
- Find each root port: the port with the lowest total path cost to the root.
- Find each designated port: for each segment, the switch with the lowest path cost to the root forwards. If tied, lowest bridge ID. Everything left over is blocked (802.1D) or discarding (802.1w).

Applying the method: S1 has the lowest MAC (0000.0CA7... is below 000A... and 0030...), so S1 is the root and all its ports forward. S2 and S3 each use their direct link to S1 as the root port (cost 4). Going through the other switch would cost 4 + 4 = 8. The last segment is S2 to S3. Both have a root path cost of 4, so the lower bridge ID forwards. S3 (000A...) beats S2 (0030...), so S3 forwards and S2 blocks its port on that link (Figure 9.5). A script confirmed this result.
Selecting the root bridge (bridge ID)

The bridge ID is 8 bytes: 2 bytes priority (0 to 65535 in the original format) + 6 bytes MAC (Figure 9.6). Compare priority first. If equal, compare MACs left to right and stop at the first difference. Lower wins. Example: 0000.0cab.3274 beats 0000.0cf6.9370. The first six hex digits are the same (0000.0c). The seventh digit is the first difference: a is lower than f, so the first switch wins. BOOK
MEMORY TIP
Compare the bridge priority first, MAC second, and always remember: lower is better for every STP value.
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS

Before the election is finished, BPDUs go out every 2 seconds on all active ports. Lowering a switch's priority makes it the root on purpose. This matters in large networks so the best path is the one chosen.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE
Small inconsistency in the book. Figure 9.3 shows S1's MAC as 0000.0CA7.A603, but the show output later (page 268) shows 0001.42A7.A603 for the same switch. The method is not affected. UPDATED
The book also writes "spanning-tree algorithm (SPA)" on page 255. The usual abbreviation is STA.
Quick check 9.1
Q1. A switch has priority 32768 in VLAN 1. What bridge priority value does show spanning-tree display?
Answer: 32769 - priority 32768 plus system ID extension 1 for VLAN 1.
Q2. Which STP states let the switch learn MAC addresses?
A. Blocking and listening
B. Learning and forwarding
C. Listening and learning
D. Forwarding only
Answer: B - MAC learning happens in learning and forwarding only.
Q3. What is the path cost for a switch with one 100 Mb/s uplink and one 1 Gb/s link beyond it to the root (short method)?
Answer: 23 - 19 + 4.
Q4. How many root ports does the root bridge have?
Answer: Zero - The root bridge has no root port; every other switch has exactly one.
Book pages 259 to 267. BOOK
| Protocol | Standard | Instances | Speed | Resources |
| 802.1D (CST) | IEEE | One for the whole network | Slow (about 50 s) | Very low |
| PVST+ (Cisco default) | Cisco | One per VLAN | Slow like CST | More than CST |
| 802.1w (RSTP) | IEEE | One for the whole network | Fast | More than CST, less than PVST+ |
| Rapid PVST+ | Cisco | One 802.1w instance per VLAN | Fast | Most CPU and memory |
| 802.1s (MSTP) | IEEE | Several VLANs mapped to each instance | Fast | Less than Rapid PVST+, but must be configured |
9.2.1 Common Spanning Tree

With CST (802.1D) there is one root bridge for all VLANs, and every switch builds one path to it (Figure 9.7). If the root switch is in the wrong place for some VLANs, traffic for those VLANs takes a poor path. You can override the root election by hand. BOOK
9.2.2 Per-VLAN Spanning Tree+

PVST+ is Cisco's extension of 802.1D. It runs a separate STP instance for each VLAN, so each VLAN can have its own root bridge placed near its servers (Figure 9.8). The cost is more CPU and memory. Convergence is still slow (about 50 s). Cisco IOS switches run 802.1D PVST+ by default. BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE
The book writes "801.2d" and "802.1 spanning-tree instance" on page 261. Both are typos for 802.1D. UPDATED
The extended system ID (why priorities move in steps of 4096)

To carry the VLAN number, PVST+ takes bits from the priority field. The priority becomes 4 bits, and the system ID extension is 12 bits (the VLAN ID). Only the top 4 bits are free to set, so priority comes in steps of 2^12 = 4096 (Figure 9.9). Bridge ID = priority (4 bits) + VLAN ID (12 bits) + MAC (6 bytes). BOOK
| Configured priority | VLAN | Value shown by show spanning-tree |
All values above were calculated by script. The 12-bit field allows VLAN IDs 0 to 4095, and there are 16 valid priorities (0, 4096, ... 61440).
EXAM CRITICAL
Review question 10 asks how many bits the sys-id-ext field has. Answer: 12. The priority part is 4 bits.
Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol 802.1w (RSTP)
In the book this sits inside the PVST+ section (pages 262 to 266). It has no tracker row of its own. BOOK

RSTP (802.1w) is an evolution of 802.1D. It converges much faster, is backward compatible, keeps most 802.1D terms, and no longer needs the 802.1D delay timers to move a port to forwarding on suitable links. It can fall back to 802.1D on a per-port basis when it hears an old switch. RSTP alone has one instance, so it does not fix poor traffic paths. Rapid PVST+ is Cisco's version that runs one 802.1w instance per VLAN. Cisco documents often say "STP" or "RSTP" but mean the PVST+ form of each. BOOK
| 802.1D state | 802.1w state |
| Disabled | Discarding |
| Blocking | Discarding |
| Listening | Discarding |
| Learning | Learning |
| Forwarding | Forwarding |
EXAM CRITICAL
RSTP has three states: discarding, learning, forwarding. It has four roles: root, designated, alternate, backup. Do not mix states and roles.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)
RSTP details the book skips (needed for the v2.0 "configure operations" wording). From Cisco's document 24062 (official):
Edge ports go straight to forwarding. This is what PortFast does. An edge port that receives a BPDU loses its edge status and becomes a normal port.
Point-to-point links (full duplex) are the second place RSTP can move rapidly to forwarding. On a shared (half-duplex) link RSTP cannot use the fast handshake.

Proposal and agreement: a switch proposes that its port should become the designated port on a link. The neighbour agrees if the proposal is better, and the port moves to forwarding quickly with no timers.
802.1D-2004 incorporated 802.1w, so the current IEEE standard for RSTP is in 802.1D, not a separate 802.1w document. CHECK for the exact current edition.
RSTP example 1 (Figure 9.10 and 9.11)

Switches SA, SB, SC, SD. Links are Fast Ethernet (100 Mb/s, cost 19) except SC to SD, which is Gigabit (cost 4). Bridge priorities are all default, so MACs decide: SC (0000.0c39.3127) is lowest and is the root. BOOK
| Switch | Root port | Path cost to root | Reason |
| SA | Fa0/0 (direct to SC) | 19 | Direct 100 Mb/s link. Via SB and SD it would be 19 + 19 + 4 = 42. |
| SB | Fa0/3 (toward SD) | 23 | Via SD: 19 + 4 = 23. Via SA: 19 + 19 = 38. |
| SD | Gi0/9 (direct to SC) | 4 | Gigabit link to the root. |

Designated ports: all ports on SC. SA Fa0/1 forwards on the SA to SB segment, and SB Fa0/2 is blocked (discarding). SD Gi0/1 forwards toward SB. A script reproduced this exact set of roles. CHECK because the topology was read from the figure.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Reasoning gap in the book (page 264). The book says SA wins the SA to SB segment "because SA has the lowest bridge ID". The real deciding factor is lowest root path cost: SA has cost 19, SB has cost 23. Bridge ID is only the tiebreaker. The final answer is the same, but the reasoning matters for harder questions. UPDATED
RSTP example 2 (Figures 9.12 to 9.14)

SC has priority 28672 (lower than the others at 32768), so SC is the root. SA has a 10 Gb/s link to SC (cost 2), so that is SA's root port. SB and SD each have a Gigabit link to SC (cost 4), which are their root ports. BOOK

Leftover segments (SA to SB and SA to SD) are decided by lowest root path cost: SA is at 2, SB and SD are at 4, so SA forwards on both and the SB and SD ports discard. A script gave the same result. CHECK (topology read from the figure)
COMMON MISTAKE

The book says (page 266): "SD has the better bridge ID (lower)". That is wrong. SA is 0021.1bee.a700 and SD is 0021.7f4b.6880. At the fifth hex digit, 1 is lower than 7, so SA has the lower MAC and the better bridge ID. The book then correctly overrides this with the path cost rule, so the final answer still stands. UPDATED (checked by script)
The four designated-port tie-break rules (book page 266)
- Lowest accumulated path cost to the root bridge.
- If tied, lowest bridge ID.

- If still tied, lowest port priority (default 128 per the show output, set with spanning-tree port-priority). The book says the default is 32768, which is wrong: the show output on page 269 shows 128.25.
- If still tied, lowest port number (Fa0/1 before Fa0/2).
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book states the default port priority is 32768 (page 266), but its own show output (Prio.Nbr 128.25) shows 128. The 32768 is the bridge priority. UPDATED Port priority values are multiples of 16 from 0 to 240 on Cisco switches. CHECK
802.1s Multiple Spanning Tree (MSTP)

MSTP maps groups of VLANs into a few instances to save CPU and memory while still converging fast like RSTP. It is useful when there are many VLANs. It does nothing until you configure region name, revision and VLAN-to-instance mapping. It is not listed in either exam outline. BOOK
Quick check 9.2
Q1. Which STP version is the Cisco IOS default?
B. PVST+ (802.1D per VLAN)
D. Rapid PVST+
Answer: B - Book page 261. Rapid PVST+ must be turned on.
Q2. How many port states does RSTP use?
Answer: Three - Discarding, learning, forwarding.
Q3. Which port role is on the same switch as the designated port for that segment?
Answer: Backup port - Alternate is on a different switch.
Q4. Two switches have equal cost to the root on a shared segment. What decides which one forwards?
Answer: Lowest bridge ID - Path cost first, then bridge ID, then port priority, then port number.

content.text: Book pages 267 to 273. BOOK Network: S1, S2, S3 in a triangle, all Gigabit (Figure 9.15). Default PVST+ on all switches.
Reading show spanning-tree
Output from the book, S1 (illustrative, not run) CHECK
S1# show spanning-tree vlan 1
VLAN0001
Spanning tree enabled protocol ieee
Root ID Priority 32769
Address 0001.42A7.A603
This bridge is the root
Hello Time 2 sec Max Age 20 sec Forward Delay 15 sec
Bridge ID Priority 32769 (priority 32768 sys-id-ext 1)
Address 0001.42A7.A603
Hello Time 2 sec Max Age 20 sec Forward Delay 15 sec
Aging Time 20
Interface Role Sts Cost Prio.Nbr Type
Gi1/1 Desg FWD 4 128.25 P2p
Gi1/2 Desg FWD 4 128.26 P2p
- protocol ieee means 802.1D (really PVST+). In Rapid PVST+ it says rstp.
- Root ID block = the root bridge for this VLAN. Bridge ID block = this switch. When they match and you see This bridge is the root, you are on the root.
- Priority 32769 (priority 32768 sys-id-ext 1) = base priority plus VLAN number.
- Interface table: Role (Root, Desg, Altn), Sts (FWD, BLK, LRN, LIS), Cost (port cost), Prio.Nbr (port priority 128 and port number), Type (P2p = point-to-point link).
- A root bridge never shows a blocked port: both ports are Desg FWD.

On S3 the Root ID block shows Cost 4 and Port 26 (GigabitEthernet1/2): the root is one Gigabit link away out of Gi1/2, and Gi1/2 is the root port (Root FWD). On S2 the output shows Gi1/1 Altn BLK and Gi1/2 Root FWD: the blocked port is S2's link to S3. BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Output formats change between IOS versions. Cisco still prints BLK for a port that Rapid PVST+ treats as discarding, and newer IOS XE shows PortFast lines as "Portfast Edge" in the summary. Confirm on your own device. UPDATED CHECK
Finding the root without a diagram
Two-step method from the book
S3# show spanning-tree
S3# show cdp neighbors
- show spanning-tree gives the root port (for example Gi1/2).
- show cdp neighbors shows which switch is connected to that port. The root is that switch or further upstream. If the Root ID cost equals one link cost (4 for Gigabit), the neighbour is the root.
Changing the root bridge
Make S2 the root for VLANs 2 and 3 CHECK
S2(config)# spanning-tree vlan 2 priority 16384
S2(config)# spanning-tree vlan 3 root primary
S2# show spanning-tree vlan 2
S2# show spanning-tree summary
- spanning-tree vlan 2 priority 16384 sets the bridge priority for VLAN 2 only. The valid range is 0 to 61440 in steps of 4096. Result shown: 16384 + 2 = 16386.
- spanning-tree vlan 3 root primary lets the switch choose a priority automatically.
- show spanning-tree vlan 2 should now say This bridge is the root.
- show spanning-tree summary lists the VLANs the switch is root for (Root bridge for: VLAN0002 VLAN0003) and the mode (pvst or rapid-pvst).
WARNING
Priority 0 always wins unless another switch is also 0. The book warns never to set every switch to 0. You must set the priority for each VLAN you want to control.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

root primary and root secondary: what they really do. root primary sets the priority to 24576 if that is enough to win. If another switch already has a lower priority, it sets its own value 4096 below the lowest root priority it sees. root secondary sets 28672. Both are one-time calculations that become fixed priority values in the config. UPDATED

Sources: Cisco NetAcad lab material and NetworkLessons (secondary), plus Cisco's Catalyst 6500 STP guide for the priority steps. The book's appendix answer to review question 2 says both commands give 16384. That is wrong. See the Gaps Log. CHECK
| Command | Priority set | When |
| spanning-tree vlan N root primary | 24576 (or 4096 below the current lowest root) | Make this switch the root |
| spanning-tree vlan N root secondary | 28672 | Make this switch the backup root |
| spanning-tree vlan N priority X | X (multiple of 4096) | Set it by hand |
MEMORY TIP
Order of value: your manual priority < primary (24576) < secondary (28672) < default (32768). Lower wins, so a switch left at default only becomes root if everything else fails or has a higher ID.
Enabling Rapid PVST+
Turn on Rapid PVST+ (global command) CHECK
S2(config)# spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
S2# show spanning-tree
S2# show spanning-tree summary
- spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst switches the whole switch to Rapid PVST+. It is one global command, not per VLAN.
- show spanning-tree now prints protocol rstp for each VLAN.
- show spanning-tree summary prints Switch is in rapid-pvst mode.
EXAM CRITICAL
Run the same STP mode on every switch. Rapid PVST+ falls back to 802.1D behaviour per port when it hears an old switch, but you then lose the fast convergence on that link.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

More show commands worth knowing ADDED CHECK : show spanning-tree root (root of every VLAN in one table), show spanning-tree interface gi0/1 detail (role, state, cost, BPDU counters), show spanning-tree blockedports (list of blocked ports), show spanning-tree inconsistentports (root guard / loop guard problems).
Quick check 9.3
Q1. A switch shows Priority 32770 (priority 32768 sys-id-ext 2). Which VLAN is this?
Answer: VLAN 2 - sys-id-ext is the VLAN ID.
Q2. Which command enables 802.1w on a Cisco switch?
A. spanning-tree mode 802.1w
B. spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
C. spanning-tree rapid enable
D. enable rstp
Answer: B - Global configuration mode.
Q3. Which command shows the VLANs for which the switch is root?
Answer: show spanning-tree summary - The Root bridge for line lists them.
Q4. Is 20000 a valid bridge priority?
Answer: No - Valid values are multiples of 4096: 20480 is valid, 20000 is not.
Book pages 273 to 275. BOOK
There are two ways STP can fail:
| Failure | What happens | Impact |
| A port is blocking when it should forward | That segment is cut off. | Limited. The rest of the network works. Easy to find. |
| A port is forwarding when it should block | A loop forms. Broadcasts, multicasts and unknown unicasts circle forever. | Severe. Can take down the whole network in seconds. |
What a loop does (book list)
- Link load climbs as more frames enter the loop. A loop inside one VLAN affects ports in that VLAN and the trunks that carry it.
- With more than one loop, frames are duplicated each time a switch floods them.
- The MAC address table becomes unstable because the same source MAC arrives on several ports.
- CPU and links hit near 100 percent. Devices become unresponsive, so you cannot even log in to troubleshoot.
Recovery (book method)
- Remove redundant links between switches one by one until the network calms down (STP then re-converges).
- Put the redundant links back one at a time, watching for the problem to return.
- Look for a failing port, a dead switch, or a link that drops BPDUs.
- When all links are back, monitor closely and have a back-out plan.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Common causes ADDED (general knowledge, CHECK ): someone plugs an unmanaged switch or hub into two wall ports, STP was disabled on a VLAN, a one-way fibre link stops BPDUs reaching a switch, mismatched duplex, or STP modes or timers differ across switches.
Protections: PortFast with BPDU Guard on access ports, root guard and loop guard on switch links (Section 9.5), UDLD on fibre, and storm control (v2.0 objective 4.7.c, a later chapter).

What the book promises: it says EtherChannel can stop ports being blocked. EtherChannel removes blocking on bundled links, but it does not replace STP: you still need STP in case of a misconfiguration.
Quick check 9.4
Q1. Which failure is worse: a port blocking wrongly or forwarding wrongly?
Answer: Forwarding wrongly - It creates a loop and a broadcast storm.
Q2. Why does the MAC table become unstable in a loop?
Answer: The same source MAC arrives on multiple ports - The table keeps changing the port for that MAC.
Q3. What is the first recovery step when the loop makes devices unresponsive?
Answer: Disconnect redundant links - Then reconnect them one at a time.
Book pages 275 to 278. BOOK

PortFast makes a port skip listening and learning and go straight to forwarding. Use it only on ports that connect to a single end device (host, server, printer), where a loop is impossible. It avoids the 30 to 50 second wait that can make DHCP fail. The book calls it a Cisco proprietary extension of 802.1D. BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Name change. In RSTP the same idea is called an edge port (it is part of the standard). Cisco's RSTP document says the PortFast keyword is used to configure edge ports. Newer IOS XE also accepts the edge keyword: spanning-tree portfast edge. Unlike old PortFast, a port that gets a BPDU loses its edge status and becomes a normal STP port. UPDATED Verified for the concept in Cisco document 24062 (official). The edge keyword syntax comes from IOS XE command documentation and a Cisco community post and was not tested. CHECK
Configuring PortFast
Global default and per-interface PortFast CHECK
S1(config)# spanning-tree portfast default
S1(config)# interface range gi0/1 - 2
S1(config-if-range)# spanning-tree portfast
S1# show spanning-tree interface gi0/1 portfast
- spanning-tree portfast default (global) turns PortFast on for all non-trunking access ports.
- interface range gi0/1 - 2 selects two ports (the book mistyped the prompts as S1#config)#).
- spanning-tree portfast (interface) enables PortFast on those ports. This is the safer, more specific way.
- spanning-tree portfast trunk allows PortFast on a trunk, only for a trunk to a server or router, never to a switch.
- show spanning-tree interface gi0/1 portfast shows whether PortFast is active. ADDED
Warning message from the book BOOK
%Warning: portfast should only be enabled on ports connected to a single
host. Connecting hubs, concentrators, switches, bridges, etc... to this
interface when portfast is enabled, can cause temporary bridging loops.
Use with CAUTION
%Portfast has been configured on GigabitEthernet0/1 but will only
have effect when the interface is in a non-trunking mode.
WHY THIS MATTERS
PortFast helps because host ports are the most common place for a slow link-up. Without it, DHCP clients can time out while the port is still listening or learning. BOOK
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)
switchport host macro ADDED CHECK : on many Catalyst models this one command sets access mode, enables PortFast, and turns off channeling. Check your platform before relying on it.
9.5.1 BPDU Guard

If a PortFast port receives a BPDU, someone connected a switch (or something that sends BPDUs). BPDU Guard puts the port into err-disabled (shutdown) state. Use it only on access-layer ports where users connect. BOOK
Global and interface BPDU Guard CHECK
S1(config)# spanning-tree portfast bpduguard default
S1(config-if)# spanning-tree bpduguard enable
S1# show interfaces status err-disabled
- spanning-tree portfast bpduguard default (global) turns BPDU Guard on for all PortFast ports.
- spanning-tree bpduguard enable (interface) turns it on for one port, even if PortFast is not on.
- show interfaces status err-disabled lists ports that were shut down. ADDED
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Recovering an err-disabled port ADDED : fix the cause first (remove the switch), then shutdown and no shutdown the port. Or enable automatic recovery with errdisable recovery cause bpduguard and errdisable recovery interval 400 (seconds). Source: Cisco document on PortFast BPDU Guard (official, general commands). CHECK
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS

The Super Bowl story (pages 277 to 278). A junior admin plugged a switch into a core port and, thinking the port was bad, tried all 24 ports on a line card. Each one tripped. The lesson is that BPDU Guard works, and that people lie about what they did. The story's setup (PortFast and BPDU Guard on links to distribution switches) is confusing, because BPDU Guard would shut a real switch uplink. In your own network use BPDU Guard only on access ports. UPDATED
Root guard and loop guard (not in the book)
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

v2.0 objective 2.5.d names root guard, loop guard and BPDU guard. The book teaches only BPDU Guard, so here is the rest. Sources: Cisco community posts and study notes on Catalyst syntax (secondary); not tested on equipment. CHECK
| Feature | Where to use it | Triggers when | Result | Recovery |
| BPDU Guard | Access ports with PortFast | Any BPDU arrives | Port goes err-disabled | Manual, or errdisable recovery |

| Root guard | Designated ports toward switches that must never be the root | A superior BPDU (one that would win the root election) arrives | Port goes root-inconsistent (blocks) | Automatic when superior BPDUs stop |

| Loop guard | Root and alternate ports on switch-to-switch links | BPDUs stop arriving on a port that was getting them | Port goes loop-inconsistent (blocks) instead of moving to forwarding | Automatic when BPDUs return |
Root guard and loop guard CHECK
S1(config-if)# spanning-tree guard root
S1(config-if)# spanning-tree guard loop
S1(config)# spanning-tree loopguard default
S1# show spanning-tree inconsistentports
- spanning-tree guard root (interface) enables root guard on that port.
- spanning-tree guard loop (interface) enables loop guard on that port.
- spanning-tree loopguard default (global) enables loop guard on all point-to-point links.
- show spanning-tree inconsistentports lists ports in root-inconsistent or loop-inconsistent state.
MEMORY TIP
Root guard = protect who is the root. Loop guard = protect against BPDUs going missing. BPDU Guard = protect access ports from switches.
Quick check 9.5
Q1. What does PortFast do?
Answer: Moves a port straight to forwarding - It skips listening and learning.
Q2. What happens when a BPDU arrives on a port with PortFast and BPDU Guard?
A. The port keeps forwarding
B. The port goes err-disabled
C. The port becomes root
D. PortFast is disabled and the port keeps working
Answer: B - The port is shut down.
Q3. Which feature stops a new switch from becoming the root by sending a superior BPDU?
Answer: Root guard - The port goes root-inconsistent.
Q4. Where should BPDU Guard be configured?
Answer: Access ports - Never on uplinks to other switches.
Book pages 278 to 283. BOOK

Most networks have several links between switches for redundancy. STP then blocks all but one. Routing protocols (OSPF, EIGRP) may see each link as a separate path. EtherChannel (port channel) bundles several physical links into one logical link. STP and routing treat the bundle as a single link, so STP does not block the extra links and there is only one routing adjacency across the bundle (Figure 9.19). BOOK
WHY THIS MATTERS
You get more bandwidth and resilience: if one member link fails, the bundle stays up with fewer links and STP does not recalculate.
Negotiation protocols and terms
| Term | Meaning |
| Port channeling | Combining several physical ports between two switches into one logical link. |
| EtherChannel | Cisco's name for port channeling. |
| PAgP | Port Aggregation Protocol. Cisco proprietary negotiation. Cisco-only. Modes: desirable and auto. The book says it sends packets every 30 seconds. |
| LACP | Link Aggregation Control Protocol. Open standard (IEEE 802.3ad, now maintained as 802.1AX). Works between vendors. Modes: active and passive. This is the one the exam tests. |
| Static (on) | Both sides forced into a channel with no negotiation. The book allows it but prefers a protocol, to catch mismatches and failures. |
| channel-group | Interface command that puts a physical port into a channel. The number is the port-channel ID. |
| interface port-channel | Creates the logical bundle interface. The number must match the channel-group number. |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Limits. The book says a bundle can have up to 8 active ports and also words this as "two-to-eight Fast Ethernet or two-Gigabit Ethernet ports", which is garbled. Cisco documentation says an LACP channel can have up to 8 active ports plus 8 standby ports (16 total); PAgP stays at 8. This is platform dependent. UPDATED Source: Cisco EtherChannel configuration guide (official, older platform); platform maximums not confirmed for current Catalyst models. CHECK
LACP standard name. 802.3ad was moved into IEEE 802.1AX. Verified only in secondary sources. CHECK
Cisco documentation also confirms that PAgP ports cannot form a channel with LACP ports. BOOK agrees.
EXAM CRITICAL
Member ports must match: same speed, same duplex, same VLAN information, same trunk settings. Configure them identically before bundling.
Which modes form a channel
| One side | Other side | Channel forms? |
| active | active | Yes |
| active | passive | Yes |
| passive | passive | No (nobody starts negotiation) |
| desirable | desirable | Yes (PAgP) |
| desirable | auto | Yes (PAgP) |
| auto | auto | No |
| on | on | Yes (static, no protocol) |
| on | active, passive, auto or desirable | No |
| LACP mode | PAgP mode | No (protocols do not mix) |
This table was generated by a script that encodes the rules and checked against Cisco's documentation for LACP and PAgP. CHECK
MEMORY TIP
Active Asks, Passive Plays along. At least one side must ask. Same with Desirable asks, Auto answers.
9.6.1 Configuring and Verifying Port Channels
Figure 9.20: S1 uses Gi0/1 and Gi0/2, S2 uses Gi0/13 and Gi0/14. BOOK
S1 configuration from the book CHECK
S1(config)# interface range g0/1 - 2
S1(config-if-range)# switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
S1(config-if-range)# switchport mode trunk
S1(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode active
S1(config-if-range)# exit
S1(config)# interface port-channel 1
S1(config-if)# switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
S1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
S1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 1,2,3
- interface range g0/1 - 2 selects both member ports so one set of commands applies to both.

- switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q sets the trunk type. Only needed on switches that support ISL as well. Many newer models (2960, Catalyst 9000) do not accept this command because they only support 802.1Q. UPDATED CHECK
- switchport mode trunk makes the members trunks. They must all match.
- channel-group 1 mode active joins the ports to channel group 1 and makes this side start LACP negotiation.
- interface port-channel 1 is the logical bundle. Settings applied here are copied to members and should match what you put on the members.
- switchport trunk allowed vlan 1,2,3 limits the VLANs the bundle carries.
S2 mirrors S1 CHECK
S2(config)# interface range g0/13 - 14
S2(config-if-range)# switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
S2(config-if-range)# switchport mode trunk
S2(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode active
S2(config-if-range)# exit
S2(config)# interface port-channel 1
S2(config-if)# switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
S2(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
S2(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 1,2,3
WARNING
Both ends need the same trunk settings and the same allowed VLAN list. A mismatch can suspend ports or leave the bundle half-formed.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)
Safer build order ADDED CHECK : shut the member ports down first, configure both ends fully, then no shutdown. This avoids a temporary loop while only one side is bundled.
Verifying
Shortened from the book (illustrative, not run) CHECK
S2# show etherchannel port-channel
Port-channel: Po1 (Primary Aggregator)
Number of ports = 2
Port state = Port-channel
Protocol = LACP
Ports in the Port-channel:
Gig0/2 Active
Gig0/1 Active
- show etherchannel port-channel gives details for each port channel: number of ports, protocol (LACP), and member ports with EC state.
- The Load column is a hexadecimal hash value used to choose a link, not the traffic load.
Summary output (illustrative) CHECK
S2# show etherchannel summary
Group Port-channel Protocol Ports
1 Po1(SU) LACP Gig0/1(P) Gig0/2(P)
| Flag | Meaning |
| S | Layer 2 port channel (L3 is R) |
| U | In use |
| D | Down |
| P | Port is in the port channel (bundled) |
| I | Stand-alone (not bundled) |
| s | Suspended (config mismatch) |
| H | Hot-standby (LACP only) |
| w | Waiting to be aggregated |
MEMORY TIP
Healthy bundle = Po1(SU) and members showing (P).
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

More verification commands ADDED CHECK : show etherchannel detail, show lacp neighbor and show lacp internal (LACP partner and local info), show interfaces port-channel 1, and show spanning-tree (the bundle appears as Po1, not as its members).
Load balancing: traffic is spread by a hash (for example port-channel load-balance src-dst-ip), so one flow stays on one link. Check with show etherchannel load-balance.
9.6.2 Layer-3 EtherChannel
Use a Layer 3 EtherChannel when connecting a switch to several ports on a router (or two multilayer switches). Put the IP address on the port-channel interface, not on the physical members. BOOK
Book example CHECK
Router(config)# interface port-channel 1
Router(config-if)# ip address 20.2.2.2 255.255.255.0
Router(config-if)# interface range g0/0 - 1
Router(config-if-range)# channel-group 1
- interface port-channel 1 creates the logical L3 interface.
- ip address 20.2.2.2 255.255.255.0 gives the bundle one address.
- interface range g0/0 - 1 selects the physical ports.
- channel-group 1 adds them. The running config then shows no ip address under each member and channel-group 1; port-channel settings are inherited by the members.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book's L3 example is incomplete for the exam. It uses a router and gives no mode. The exam objective (v1.1 2.4 and v2.0 2.1.c) is about Layer 3 EtherChannel between multilayer switches or switch-to-router with LACP. On a multilayer switch you need no switchport on the members and the port-channel, and an LACP mode. UPDATED Whether a given router model supports EtherChannel depends on the platform. CHECK
Layer 3 EtherChannel on a multilayer switch ADDED CHECK
SW1(config)# interface range g1/0/1 - 2
SW1(config-if-range)# no switchport
SW1(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode active
SW1(config-if-range)# exit
SW1(config)# interface port-channel 1
SW1(config-if)# no switchport
SW1(config-if)# ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252
SW1# show etherchannel summary
- no switchport turns each port (and the port-channel) into a routed port.
- channel-group 1 mode active bundles with LACP.
- ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252 is a /30 point-to-point link address (a /30 has 2 usable hosts, calculated by script). The other end uses 10.1.1.2.
- show etherchannel summary should show Po1(RU): R = Layer 3, U = in use.
Quick check 9.6
Q1. Which LACP mode combination will not form a channel?
A. active/active
B. active/passive
C. passive/passive
D. passive/active
Answer: C - Neither side starts negotiation.
Q2. Which protocol is the open standard: PAgP or LACP?
Answer: LACP - PAgP is Cisco proprietary.
Q3. Which flags show a healthy Layer 2 port channel in show etherchannel summary?
Answer: SU for the port channel and P for members - S = Layer 2, U = in use, P = bundled.
Q4. Where do you configure the IP address of a Layer 3 EtherChannel?
Answer: On the port-channel interface - Members stay with no ip address.

labs.title: Watch the default STP elect a root

content.text: - Add three Catalyst 2960 switches S1, S2, S3. Connect S1 Fa0/1 to S2 Fa0/1, S2 Fa0/2 to S3 Fa0/2, and S3 Fa0/1 to S1 Fa0/2 with crossover cables (a triangle).
- Wait until all ports turn green. On each switch run show spanning-tree.
- Write down each switch's Bridge ID (priority and MAC). Predict the root before reading the output, then check.
- On every switch note the role and state of each interface.
- show spanning-tree shows root ID, bridge ID, and a role/state table for each VLAN. VLAN 1 is the only one present by default.
MEMORY TIP

Expected result: the switch with the lowest MAC (all priorities are 32769) is the root and all its ports are Desg FWD. Each other switch has one Root FWD port (direct link, cost 19). The link between the two non-root switches has one forwarding port (the lower bridge ID) and one Altn BLK port. Why: FastEthernet costs 19, and both non-root switches have a root path cost of 19, so bridge ID breaks the tie. CHECK

labs.title: Control the root and turn on Rapid PVST+

content.text: - Using the Lab 1 topology, make all three inter-switch links trunks and create VLANs 10 and 20 on every switch.
- Configure the roots as shown below.
- Run spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst on all three switches.
- Verify with show spanning-tree vlan 10, show spanning-tree vlan 20 and show spanning-tree summary.
- Test failure: on S1 shut down both uplinks (shutdown) and look at the roots again.
Commands (repeat the VLAN, trunk and mode steps on S2 and S3 with their own port numbers) CHECK
S1(config)# vlan 10
S1(config-vlan)# vlan 20
S1(config-vlan)# exit
S1(config)# interface range fa0/1 - 2
S1(config-if-range)# switchport mode trunk
S1(config-if-range)# exit
S1(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 root primary
S1(config)# spanning-tree vlan 20 root secondary
S2(config)# spanning-tree vlan 20 root primary
S2(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 root secondary
S1(config)# spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
- vlan 10 and vlan 20 create the VLANs. STP builds one instance per VLAN, so a VLAN must exist.
- switchport mode trunk carries all VLANs on the inter-switch ports.
- root primary and root secondary set priorities automatically, as explained in 9.3.
- spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst must be run on all three switches.
MEMORY TIP

Expected result: VLAN 10 root = S1 with priority 24586 (24576 + 10); S2 is next best at 28682 (28672 + 10). VLAN 20 root = S2 with 24596; S1 at 28692. show spanning-tree summary says rapid-pvst and each root lists its VLANs. After shutting S1's uplinks, S2 becomes the root for VLAN 10 because 28682 beats the default 32778. The numbers assume the other switch is left at the default and were calculated by hand. CHECK
- On S1 connect a PC to Fa0/10. Enable PortFast and BPDU Guard on that port.
- Unplug and replug the PC and watch how fast the port turns green.
- Add a fourth switch S4 and connect it to S1 Fa0/10 in place of the PC.
- Run show interfaces status and show spanning-tree interface fa0/10.
- Fix it: remove S4, then shutdown and no shutdown on Fa0/10.
Commands CHECK
S1(config)# interface fa0/10
S1(config-if)# switchport mode access
S1(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast
S1(config-if)# spanning-tree bpduguard enable
S1# show interfaces status
S1(config-if)# shutdown
S1(config-if)# no shutdown
- switchport mode access makes it an end-device port (PortFast has no effect on a trunk unless you use trunk).
- spanning-tree portfast skips listening and learning.
- spanning-tree bpduguard enable shuts the port if a BPDU arrives.
- shutdown and no shutdown clear the err-disabled state once the cause is gone.
MEMORY TIP

Expected result: with PortFast the link goes green almost immediately. When S4 is attached the port shows err-disabled and a log message appears. After removing S4 and bouncing the port, it comes back. Packet Tracer may not reproduce the log messages or timing exactly. CHECK
- Build two switches S1 and S2 with two cables: S1 Fa0/3 to S2 Fa0/3 and S1 Fa0/4 to S2 Fa0/4.
- Before bundling, run show spanning-tree and note that one link is blocked.
- Configure both ends: S1 active, S2 passive.
- Verify with show etherchannel summary and show spanning-tree.
- Change S1 to passive (both passive) and see what happens. Then set both to active.
Commands CHECK
S1(config)# interface range fa0/3 - 4
S1(config-if-range)# switchport mode trunk
S1(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode active
S2(config)# interface range fa0/3 - 4
S2(config-if-range)# switchport mode trunk
S2(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode passive
S1# show etherchannel summary
- interface range fa0/3 - 4 configures both members at once.
- switchport mode trunk makes both members the same trunk type.
- channel-group 1 mode active and mode passive select LACP and who starts negotiation.
MEMORY TIP

Expected result: show etherchannel summary shows Po1(SU) with Fa0/3(P) Fa0/4(P), and show spanning-tree lists Po1 only, no blocked link. With passive on both ends the bundle does not form and the members are stand-alone (or STP blocks one). If Packet Tracer rejects LACP modes, note the PT version and repeat the lab on another simulator. CHECK
- Use two multilayer switches (for example 3560 or 3650 in Packet Tracer). Connect two links between them.
- On both switches: no switchport on the two members, channel-group 1 mode active, then configure interface port-channel 1 with no switchport and an IP address.
- Use 10.1.1.1/30 on SW1 and 10.1.1.2/30 on SW2, then ping from each side.
- Run show etherchannel summary and show ip interface brief.
MEMORY TIP
Expected result: Po1(RU) with both members (P), and successful pings. Not every Packet Tracer device or version supports Layer 3 port channels. If yours rejects it, do this as a paper lab. CHECK

Paper lab 1. Four switches W, X, Y, Z. Priorities: X = 24576, all others 32768. MACs: W 0000.1111.1111, X 0000.2222.2222, Y 0000.0AAA.0001, Z 0000.3333.3333. Links: X-W (1G), X-Y (100M), W-Z (1G), Y-Z (1G), W-Y (100M). Find the root, each root port, and which ports block. Then change X to 32768 and find the new root.
MEMORY TIP

Answer (calculated by script): root = X (lowest priority). Root path costs: W 4, Z 8, Y 12. Root ports: W via the X link, Z via the W link, Y via the Z link (12 beats 19 via X and 23 via W). Y's ports toward X and W block (alternate). If X is set to 32768, root = Y (MAC 0000.0AAA... is lowest). Topology and costs are from this document; not run on equipment. CHECK
Paper lab 2. Three Gigabit switches P (priority 4096), Q and R (both 32768, MACs 0000.BBBB.0002 and 0000.CCCC.0003). Links: P-Q, P-R, Q-R. Which port blocks?
MEMORY TIP
Answer (script): P is the root. Q and R each have cost 4 to the root. On the Q-R segment both have equal cost, so the lower bridge ID wins: Q forwards, R blocks its port toward Q. CHECK
